content: The implementation of recommendations for managing HIV and tuberculosis (TB) can be enhanced by integrating services, as discussed in Chapter 9. HIV and hepatitis B virus (HBV) coinfection significantly impacts the natural progression of HBV infection. This includes higher rates of chronic HBV infection, reduced spontaneous clearance of HBV, accelerated liver fibrosis progression, increased risks of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, higher liver-related mortality, and diminished antiretroviral (ARV) therapy response. Liver disease has become a leading cause of death in individuals coinfected with HIV and HBV. The 2010 WHO antiretroviral therapy (ART) guidelines recommended initiating ART for all individuals coinfected with HIV and HBV who require treatment for chronic active hepatitis, regardless of CD4 cell count or WHO clinical stage. However, due to the lack of routine HBV screening, many individuals are unaware of their HBV status. Additionally, access to expensive diagnostic tools for liver disease staging, such as liver biopsy, transient elastography, HBV-DNA testing, and serum biomarkers, is limited. These tools are essential for identifying chronic active liver disease and determining eligibility for HBV treatment. A meta-analysis and subgroup analysis of a randomized controlled trial provided low-quality evidence on the overall impact of ART on liver-related morbidity and mortality in individuals coinfected with HIV and HBV. However, these studies did not evaluate the benefits of initiating ART at higher CD4 counts. The Guidelines Development Group concluded that there was insufficient evidence or a favorable risk-benefit profile to support initiating ART in all individuals coinfected with HIV and HBV with CD4 counts >500 cells/mm³ or regardless of CD4 count or liver disease stage. Early ART initiation carries risks such as hepatotoxicity, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, and hepatic flares. Nevertheless, the Guidelines Development Group recommends providing ART to all individuals coinfected with HIV and HBV who have evidence of severe chronic liver disease, as they are at the highest risk of liver disease progression and mortality. The term severe chronic liver disease was used instead of chronic active hepatitis to ensure broader understanding and applicability based on clinical criteria alone. In settings where ART cannot be provided to all individuals with HIV and CD4 counts ≤500 cells/mm³, priority should be given to diagnosing and treating those coinfected with HIV and HBV. Data from a randomized controlled trial support the use of at least two agents with activity against HBV (e.g., tenofovir disoproxil fumarate [TDF] plus lamivudine [3TC] or emtricitabine [FTC]) to improve viral load response and reduce the development of HBV drug resistance. Critical research gaps include the need for more data on the impact of ART on liver-related outcomes in HBV-coinfected individuals in resource-limited settings and the relative impact of ART in individuals with CD4 counts >500 cells/mm³ and early-stage liver disease. For individuals with HIV who are 50 years or older, pooled data from 13 cohorts in Europe and North America showed an increased risk of death and disease progression. However, these data were not stratified by CD4 count and do not support initiating ART at CD4 counts >500 cells/mm³ for this group. For individuals with HIV-2, the lack of randomized treatment studies makes it challenging to determine the optimal timing of ART initiation. Observational data from 15 studies showed no significant differences in outcomes between initiating ART at CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³ and >350 cells/mm³, but the quality of evidence was rated as low to very low due to bias and imprecision. The Guidelines Development Group endorsed the principle that initiating ART among people coinfected with hepatitis C virus (HCV) should follow the same principles as in HIV monoinfection. However, initiating ART regardless of CD4 count was not recommended due to insufficient evidence. Challenges in diagnosing and treating active HCV infection in resource-limited settings include limited access to HCV antibody and RNA assays, diagnostic tools for liver disease staging, and HCV therapy. Despite these challenges, limited access to HCV testing or treatment should not be a barrier to initiating ART. WHO hepatitis guidelines forthcoming in 2014 will provide detailed guidance on HCV screening, treatment, and care. People coinfected with HIV and HCV who are receiving ART and HCV drugs require close monitoring due to potential drug interactions and increased risks of drug toxicity between HCV drugs (e.g., interferon, ribavirin, and newer directly acting agents) and ARV drugs. The 2013 WHO guidelines recommend ART for all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV during the period of risk for mother-to-child HIV transmission and continuing lifelong ART either for all women or for those meeting eligibility criteria for their own health. Option A is no longer recommended. The advantages of a standardized ARV regimen for all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV include ease of implementation, harmonized regimens, increased ART coverage, prevention of vertical transmission, maternal health benefits, and strong community acceptability. ART also reduces sexual transmission of HIV to partners. The Guidelines Development Group considered evidence from systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials in evaluating when to start ART in adults. The recommendation to increase ART use in pregnant and breastfeeding women acknowledges limited ARV drug options in resource-limited countries and balances the benefits of starting ART with potential risks of ARV drug toxicity to the mother, fetus, and infant during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Other considerations include costs, cost-effectiveness, health system burden, adherence, retention, and the prevention benefits of immediate ART initiation.
